notes.b: Ventilation is the continuous replacement of stale indoor air with fresh air. A well-ventilated home stays healthy and dry, and it does this without causing a draught or lowering the room temperature much.
points: Ventilation supplies fresh air (oxygen) for breathing and for the combustion (burning) of fuel in open fires, stoves and gas appliances, because a flame needs a steady air supply.
It removes stale air, carbon dioxide and impurities, together with moist air and cooking smells, so rooms stay fresh and the spread of infection is reduced.
It controls humidity (the amount of water vapour in the air) and temperature, so rooms do not become hot, damp and stuffy.
It prevents condensation, mould and damp, which damage the fabric (the structure and finishes) of the house and can aggravate asthma and bronchitis.
Modern airtight construction, insulation, double glazing, tight-fitting doors and windows and sealed fireplaces reduce natural air flow, so artificial methods are often needed.
Part F (Ventilation) of the Building Regulations requires adequate ventilation in new homes.
Fresh air should be introduced without causing a draught or lowering the room temperature, because the aim is controlled air change and not lost heat.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the importance of adequate ventilation as a list of points: fresh air, removes stale air and smells, controls humidity and temperature, reduces condensation, and aids combustion. Make each point a separate, clear statement. Remember that ventilation is controlled, while a draught is uncontrolled cold air that wastes heat.

notes.b: When stale air cannot escape, moisture, heat and smells collect indoors. The most obvious results are stuffy rooms and condensation, and the longer-term results are damp, damage to the house and health problems.
points: Air becomes stale and stuffy, with high humidity and lingering smells, because nothing is replacing it.
Condensation forms on cold surfaces such as windows, external walls and room corners, which leads to damp, mould and mildew, peeling paint and wallpaper, rotting wood and rusting metal.
Persistent damp causes structural damage to walls, ceilings and window frames, and wet insulation insulates less well.
Respiratory conditions such as asthma and bronchitis, and allergies, get worse in damp, mouldy air.
Kitchens and bathrooms suffer steam, heat, grease and smells, which collect and create overheating and slippery floors.
Gases can build up as a secondary effect: carbon dioxide rises and the oxygen supply falls, causing headaches and tiredness.
Combustion appliances that are not properly vented are starved of air and burn incompletely, which can produce carbon monoxide.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for the effects of poor or inadequate ventilation. Lead with stuffy air, condensation, mould, damp and smells, and add asthma, and overheating and slippery floors for a kitchen. Give gas build-up as an extra point. Remember that a lack of air makes combustion incomplete, and that is what produces carbon monoxide.

notes.b: Air only moves when something drives it. Two forces do this in a home, and the principle you give must match the method you name. A flue is a third idea, because it carries waste gases away from burning fuel.
points: Convection: warm air is less dense (lighter), so it rises to high outlets, while cooler fresh air enters through low openings to replace it, producing a circulation that exchanges the air.

Suction (a pressure difference): an extractor fan lowers the air pressure inside a room, so stale air is drawn out and fresh air enters through openings such as vents and gaps under doors to replace it.
Wind and cross-ventilation: wind moving across the outside of a building creates pressure differences, so air enters on the windward side and leaves on the opposite side.
Combustion appliances need a steady air supply, and a flue (a chimney or pipe) carries their waste gases up and out of the house by convection as the hot gases rise.
notes.tip: The 2025 higher level question asked for the underlying principle: convection (warm air rises, cooler air replaces it) or suction for a fan. State the principle for the method you name, because naming a fan alone does not earn the principle marks.

notes.b: Natural methods use openings in the building and the movement of air through them, so they need no electricity. They are simple, but they depend on conditions outside.
points: Windows and doors are the simplest method: a window open at the top and bottom gives convection, and opening windows on opposite sides of a room gives cross-ventilation and the greatest air change.
Air bricks and wall vents are openings in external walls that let air into and out of a room. High and low openings give an exchange of air, and they must never be blocked.
Trickle vents are small adjustable slots in window frames that let fresh air in continuously at a low, slow rate, so rooms are ventilated without opening a window.
Chimneys, fireplaces and flues: an open fire draws air into the room and carries smoke up the chimney as the hot gases rise.
Natural ventilation depends on the weather, wind and season, so the air change is not constant, and it can cause draughts and heat loss. It cannot be relied on to give a steady air supply.
Diagram: cross-section of a room showing warm, stale air rising out of a high vent and cooler fresh air entering through a low air brick.
notes.tip: Past papers ask for a natural method and an artificial method, each with its principle. For a natural method such as a window, an air brick, a vent or a flue, name it and explain the principle, such as convection or cross-ventilation.

notes.b: Artificial methods use electric fans, so they give a more reliable air change in places where moisture and smells are made. Modern airtight homes need them because natural air flow is limited.
points: Extractor fan: an electric motor turns the blades, which create suction and draw out stale air, steam and smells. Shutters open when the fan runs and close when it is switched off, and fresh air flows in through gaps, under doors or through vents.

Extractor fans are fitted high on an external wall, in the ceiling or in a window, and are placed in kitchens, bathrooms and toilets, where moisture and smells are produced. They can be controlled by a switch, pull cord, timer or humidity sensor.
Ducted cooker hood: a motor drives a fan that draws air up through grease filters and expels it outside through a duct, so it removes steam and heat as well as grease.

Ductless cooker hood: filters trap grease and fumes, and the cleaned air is recirculated into the room. It does not remove moisture or heat, so it does not reduce steam. Filters need cleaning or replacing.

Mechanical ventilation system: a duct system in the ceiling or floor, in which fans blow fresh air in and remove stale air. Heat-recovery versions warm the incoming air using heat from the outgoing air, and the system suits airtight houses.
Air conditioning is an alternative that also controls humidity and temperature, but it is unusual in Irish homes.
For a kitchen, recommend an extractor fan or a ducted cooker hood plus a window or trickle vent, giving the principle of suction and the replacement of air.
Diagram: an extractor fan in an external wall with shutters, and a ducted cooker hood with its duct running to the outside.
notes.tip: For an artificial method, name it (3 to 4 marks in past papers) and explain how it works: for an extractor fan, the motor spins the blades, the shutters open, suction removes stale air and fresh air replaces it. A ductless hood recirculates air and does not remove steam, whereas a ducted hood or extractor fan does.

notes.b: Condensation is the most common ventilation problem in homes. It is not caused by damp walls: it is water vapour from the air turning to liquid on a cold surface.
points: Warm air holds more water vapour than cold air, so when warm, moist air touches a cold surface it cools and its water vapour turns to liquid water.
Everyday sources of moisture are cooking, kettles, bathing and showers, drying clothes indoors, breathing, and unflued gas or paraffin heaters.

Effects include damp patches, mould growth on walls and ceilings, peeling paint and wallpaper, rust, rotting wood and window frames, musty smells and respiratory problems. Damp insulation also loses its effect.
Prevention: ventilate with extractor fans, trickle vents and open windows, and keep lids on pots so less steam escapes.
Dry clothes outdoors or in a well-ventilated room, and keep the heating steady so surfaces do not get cold.
Insulation and double glazing keep surfaces warm, so water vapour has no cold surface to condense on. Wipe off condensation and keep furniture away from walls.
notes.tip: The 2015 higher level question on condensation asked for effects and prevention, three points each. Effects: mould, rusting, rotting wood, damp insulation, musty smells, respiratory problems. Prevention: warm the surface, reduce moisture, and ventilate.

notes.h: Practical context: evaluating ventilation at home or in the home economics room
notes.b: You may be asked to judge how well a room is ventilated and to recommend improvements. Look for the signs of poor air change first, then check what is provided to deal with it.
points: Assess ventilation by noting smells, stuffiness, condensation on windows and any mould or damp in corners.
Check which vents, air bricks and extractor fans are present and whether they are working and not blocked, because a blocked vent gives no air change.

Recommend improvements such as an extractor fan or cooker hood over the cooker, trickle vents in windows, keeping the kitchen door closed while cooking so steam does not spread, and moving clothes drying indoors to a ventilated space.
notes.tip: For a practical evaluation, name what you observed and then link each recommendation to the principle, such as suction for the fan and replacement of air.

keyTerms.definition: The supply of fresh air to a room and removal of stale, moist or polluted air from it.
Air movement through openings such as windows, vents and chimneys, driven by wind and by temperature differences.
Air movement produced by a fan or powered system, such as an extractor fan or a mechanical ventilation system.
An electric fan fitted in a wall, ceiling or window that removes stale, moist air by suction.
A perforated brick or grille set in an external wall to let air into a room or underfloor space.
A small adjustable vent in a window frame that allows a continuous low flow of fresh air.
Air flowing through a room from one opening to another on the opposite side, giving a high rate of air change.
Water that forms when warm, moist air cools on a cold surface and its water vapour turns to liquid.
The amount of water vapour held in the air, which rises when cooking, bathing and drying clothes indoors.
The burning of fuel, which needs a steady supply of oxygen and produces waste gases that must be vented.

factCards.term: Four ways air moves without a fan
factCards.definition: Opening windows and doors, air bricks, trickle vents in window frames, and a chimney or flue used with an open fire.
It provides fresh air and removes stale air, controls humidity and temperature, and prevents condensation, mould and damp.
Ducted, which expels air outside through a duct, and ductless, which filters the air and returns it to the room.
Condensation with mould and damp, a build-up of carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide, and worsened asthma and bronchitis.

factCards.term: Two ways warm air moves through a room with natural ventilation
factCards.definition: Warm air rises and leaves through high outlets, and cooler air enters through low openings.

factCards.term: Two places an extractor fan is commonly fitted
factCards.definition: In an external wall or ceiling, and in kitchens and bathrooms where moisture and smells are produced.

questions.prompt: Outline three effects of inadequate ventilation in a kitchen.
questions.model: Any three of: lingering cooking smells and stale air (2 marks); condensation on cold surfaces leading to damp and mould (2 marks); overheating and slippery floors from steam and heat that cannot escape (2 marks). Also accepted: a build-up of carbon monoxide from a gas cooker that is not properly vented.

questions.prompt: Recommend one natural method and one artificial method of ventilating a kitchen. For each method, name it and explain its underlying principle.
questions.model: Natural method: opening a window or using an air brick or trickle vent. Principle: convection, as warm, moist air rises and leaves through a high opening while cooler fresh air enters through a low opening, producing an exchange of air driven by temperature differences and wind. Artificial method: an extractor fan or a ducted cooker hood placed over the cooker. Principle: an electric motor turns blades that create suction, drawing steam, fumes and odours out of the room; shutters or the duct carry the air outside, and fresh air replaces it through openings. A ductless hood instead passes the air through grease and odour filters and returns it to the room.
